title: A secret shift with a loud letter
hook: Move every letter by a secret amount. The message still gives the key away.

knows: letters as positions in the alphabet
doesNotKnow: that a cipher which keeps letter patterns leaks its key

misconception: A message shifted by a secret amount is unreadable without the key.
objective: The learner can explain that a Caesar shift renames letters but keeps their counts, so lining up the most common cipher letter with E finds the shift (here X, shift 19) without trying all 25 keys.

claims.text: X is 19 places after E, so a shift that turns E into X is a shift of 19.
claims.source: Alphabet positions from 0: E = 4, X = 23; 23 - 4 = 19. Checked in node by the builder.

claims.text: E is the most common letter in English.
claims.source: Lewand, Cryptological Mathematics (MAA, 2000), English letter frequency table: E about 12.7%, the highest. Statement is about typical English text, not every sentence.

claims.text: In the lesson's message, E is the most common letter (23 of 94 letters), so after the shift of 19 the most common cipher letter is X, and lining the tallest bar up with E gives the right shift on the first try.
claims.source: Builder's node count of the plaintext in Demo.tsx (PLAIN): E 23, T 13, H 9 of 94 letters; cipher top letter X (23). The message was written for the lesson and over-represents E (24% against about 13% in typical English); disclosed as a chosen example.

claims.text: Shifting renames letters but keeps how often each appears.
claims.source: A Caesar shift is a one-to-one map from letters to letters applied to every position, so each cipher letter appears exactly as often as the plain letter it stands for.

claims.text: A Caesar cipher has only 25 shifts to try.
claims.source: 26 letters give shifts 0..25; shift 0 leaves the text unchanged, leaving 25 non-trivial keys.

claims.text: Al-Kindi described frequency analysis in the 9th century.
claims.source: Singh, The Code Book (1999), ch. 1: al-Kindi's 'A Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages', 9th century.

recall.question: A long English message was encrypted with a Caesar shift. Its most common letter is H. What is the shift most likely to be?
options: It cannot be guessed without the key
recall.why: The most common cipher letter is probably E in disguise. H is 3 places after E, so the shift is probably 3.
